questions.question: Explain why governments pursue industrial development deliberately, using the concepts of value added, beneficiation, linkages and stability — and state the standing caution that must accompany any support programme.
questions.expected_answer: Industrial development expands manufacturing relative to raw-material extraction. Governments pursue it because each processing stage adds value — iron ore becomes steel, steel becomes components, components become a vehicle — and the country performing those stages keeps the wages, profits and taxes they generate; performing them before export is beneficiation. Manufacturing absorbs semi-skilled labour on a scale mining and finance cannot, addressing mass unemployment. A diversified industrial base stabilises an economy otherwise exposed to swings in world commodity prices. And factories create linkages: backward linkages to suppliers such as component makers and transporters, and forward linkages to dealers and users of their output, so one plant supports hundreds of firms. The caution is the infant-industry problem: protection and subsidies tax consumers and the budget, so support must be conditional and temporary — aimed at industries becoming competitive, not merely comfortable — or it breeds permanent dependants, as apartheid's homeland decentralisation factories demonstrated when they collapsed once subsidies stopped.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's main industrial and regional development instruments by name, distinguishing zone-based from corridor-based approaches.
questions.expected_answer: Under the National Industrial Policy Framework of 2007, rolling Industrial Policy Action Plans target priority sectors. Key instruments: the Automotive Production and Development Programme, rewarding local vehicle production and investment through duty credits and allowances; the Clothing and Textiles Competitiveness Programme; Section 12I tax allowances for large industrial investments; the Black Industrialists Scheme linking industrial policy to transformation; finance through the Industrial Development Corporation; and localisation, requiring state entities to procure designated products locally. Regionally, Special Economic Zones — created from the earlier Industrial Development Zones by the SEZ Act of 2014 — are purpose-built industrial areas near ports and airports offering a 15 percent corporate tax rate, building allowances, employment tax incentives and duty-free inputs for export production; named zones include Coega with the deep-water port of Ngqura, East London, Richards Bay, Dube TradePort, Saldanha Bay and Tshwane. Corridor-based Spatial Development Initiatives instead concentrate investment along routes with economic potential — the flagship Maputo Development Corridor upgraded the N4, rail and border links between Gauteng and Maputo's port through public-private partnership, lifting activity along the whole route rather than at one fenced site.

questions.question: Evaluate the appropriateness of South Africa's industrial and regional strategies against international best practice, citing named successes and failures and reaching a defensible verdict.
questions.expected_answer: Best practice from successful industrialisers ties support to export performance, keeps it temporary and conditional, and invests in skills, infrastructure and macroeconomic stability alongside. Measured against this, the APDP scores well — support depends on producing and exporting competitively, and seven global manufacturers assemble vehicles here, ranking among top manufactured exports. Coega and Dube TradePort show genuine tenants, jobs and cargo, and the Maputo Corridor moves real freight. Against these wins stand failures: manufacturing's share of GDP has fallen from over 19 percent toward 12 to 13 percent — deindustrialisation; clothing employment collapsed despite support; and several zones remain largely empty, with public investment not followed by private money. The strongest evaluation point is binding constraints: incentives cannot compensate for unreliable electricity, congested ports, failing rail and scarce skills, so sequencing infrastructure repair may matter more than any subsidy. Cost and governance complete the test — rands per sustainable job, clean procurement and policy certainty are themselves location factors. Verdict: the direction and flagship programmes are appropriate, but the strategy underperforms while network foundations crumble; fixing the constraints is the precondition for the incentives to bite.
